title: Papa Leone XIV torna in Sudamerica: il viaggio di 12 giorni dopo l'intervento
text: Papa Leone XIV torna in Sudamerica: il viaggio di 12 giorni dopo l'intervento Inizia oggi il tour di 12 giorni di Papa Leone XIV in Uruguai, Perù e Argentina, un viaggio che rappresenta una prova di resistenza fisica dopo l'operazione ai polmoni e un ritorno in una regione fondamentale per la Chiesa Cattolica. Nonostante la recente chirurgia per un tumore, il Papa mantiene il programma originale con oltre 50 impegni e 30.000 chilometri da percorrere, confermando la presenza anche ad alta quota a Cuzco. It is a homecoming. It is a stress test for his pontificate following his recent lung operation. And it is a journey into a region that is both a religious stronghold — Latin America is home to the largest share of the world's Catholics — and a politically turbulent landscape. These are the three defining themes of Pope Leo XIV’s visit to Uruguay, Peru and Argentina, which begins today and runs until 17 November. Over 12 days, Robert Francis Prevost will travel more than 30,000 kilometres, visit 14 locations, take numerous flights by plane and helicopter, attend more than 50 engagements and deliver around 40 speeches.It is a demanding, tightly packed schedule that Leo XIV was determined not to alter after undergoing successful surgery on 13 October to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung. The Pope himself wanted the operation scheduled in time for the trip, which had already been arranged. After being discharged from Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, he gradually resumed work and public appearances, although he did forgo some engagements, including a helicopter trip to Assisi.Only after receiving favourable test results and clearance from his doctors did the Holy See confirm, on 26 October, that the Pontiff would indeed make the journey “according to the previously published programme”. All the stops have therefore been confirmed, including those that had caused some concern even among Latin American cardinals, such as the visit to Cuzco, Peru, an Indigenous city situated more than 3,000 metres above sea level.Routine medical care “The plan remains unchanged,” Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni told a briefing, appearing alongside Montse Alvarado, the young Mexican-born American who has headed the Vatican’s communications department since 1 November.“Ordinary medical care is considered sufficient,” Bruni said, explaining that there would be “no special arrangements or equipment”. “The Pope has fantastic stamina,” Alvarado added. “You saw him at Mass yesterday. He sings in a way that you can only sing if you have very strong lungs.The Pope is grateful for the concern and affection. We have everything we need, but the doctors are very confident and he is in excellent health. ” As on previous trips, the Pope will be accompanied by his personal physician, Luigi Carboni, and nurses, while an ambulance will also be part of the entourage.Construction work on the stage where Pope Leo XIV will celebrate Mass at Las Palmas Air Base in Lima, Peru “I am happy to be returning to the continent where I spent so many moments of my life,” the Pope said. Born in Chicago 71 years ago, Robert Francis Prevost spent more than 20 years of his life in northern Peru, first as a young missionary — in Chulucanas in 1985, then in Trujillo from 1988 to 1999 — and later as bishop of Chiclayo, from 2014 to 2023.As superior general of the Augustinian order from 2001 to 2013, he also visited several Latin American countries, including Argentina, where he met the then archbishop of Buenos Aires, Jorge Mario Bergoglio, with whom he initially had some disagreements. After becoming Pope, Francis appointed him first as a bishop in Peru and later brought him to Rome to head the Vatican department responsible for selecting bishops around the world.Francis never concealed his fondness for this “American, yes, but from the south”, as he liked to put it. Latin America is home to 575 million Catholics, more than 40% of the worldwide total. According to figures from the Pew Research Center, however, the proportion of people identifying as Catholic has declined over the past decade, while the number of non-believers has risen. Evangelical Protestantism, meanwhile, has been growing for decades.Apart from the recent victory of Luiz Inácio “Lula” da Silva in Brazil, relatively few countries are now governed by left-wing politicians — Mexico, Guatemala, Guyana, Suriname, Uruguay and Cuba — while the radical and populist right has come to power in many others, including Ecuador, Colombia, Bolivia, Honduras, Chile, Costa Rica and Peru, as well as Argentina before them.“May this journey be an opportunity to open our hearts to one another,” the Pope said, “strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy! ”Pope Leo begins his visit in Uruguay, Latin America’s most secularised country, with a history also marked by a degree of anticlericalism. So much so that, as Vatican News recently recalled, Christmas is known as Family Day and Holy Week as Tourism Week.Welcomed by the left-wing president Yamandú Orsi, the Pope will spend 48 hours in the country, visiting both the capital, Montevideo, and Paysandú, where he will celebrate Mass among rural communities on Saturday, 7 November. As well as meeting government officials, bishops and representatives of Uruguayan society, he will visit the Catholic university and preside over an evening vigil at the capital’s stadium. The second leg of the journey, from Sunday to Wednesday, takes the Pope to Argentina.It is the homeland of Jorge Mario Bergoglio, who never returned to his native country as Pope, prompting questions and some resentment. That is one more reason why Argentine Catholics are eagerly awaiting the visit: they have not welcomed a Pope to their country since John Paul II travelled there in 1987. Leo will be greeted by President Javier Milei, a figure of the far right who initially insulted Francis, accusing him of being a “communist” and an “imbecile”.Once in office, however, Milei repaired relations with the Pope. Francis welcomed him with open arms because, as La Nación put it, “you have to plough with the oxen you have”. Milei’s policies dismantling the welfare state in recent years have increased poverty and inequality, drawing open criticism from the Argentine Catholic Church. For this reason, the government has organised the visit amid concerns that Leo might raise issues or meet people who could amplify those criticisms.Milei has embraced its development, announcing his intention not to regulate it, while in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, Leo strongly calls for regulation and warns of the risks. Peter Thiel, one of the leading figures of the American tech right, has also recently moved to Buenos Aires. Obsessed with the figure of the Antichrist, Thiel has described Leo as a “woke pope” and a “useful idiot” of the Chinese communist government.Santo Toribio de Mogrovejo Church in Zaña, northern Peru, with a banner bearing an image of Pope Leo XIV hanging from one of its towers In Argentina, Leo will visit Buenos Aires, Córdoba, in the east of the country, and Luján, near the capital, home to a famous Marian shrine. Among other things, Leo will visit the “Little Cottolengo”, a facility caring for people with disabilities and those struggling with drug addictions.He will also meet representatives of business, trade unions and grassroots movements, whom he has already received at the Vatican, on Monday. On Tuesday, he will preside over a vigil with young people at the Monumento de los Españoles, before visiting a prison on Wednesday. Although it is smaller than Argentina, the Pope will spend six days there.He will be welcomed by the new president, Keiko Fujimori, daughter of former president and dictator Alberto Fujimori, who ruled the country from 1990 to 2000 using increasingly authoritarian methods. As reconstructed by both Elise Allen, in the only book-length interview with the Pope, and Daniel Burke and Scott Detrow in their biography, Prevost remained in Peru as a missionary despite death threats against American priests from the left-wing terrorist movement Shining Path.At the same time, he quietly encouraged petitions and demonstrations against human rights violations committed by the Fujimori regime. The new president, who took office only a few months ago, has announced a military-led security crackdown to combat drug cartels and the criminal networks surrounding them. Another emergency is looming over the country: El Niño, the exceptional weather phenomenon that threatens floods, droughts and major disruption to the fishing industry.For the Pope, returning to Peru means coming home and offering the world a tangible expression of his vision of a Church committed to society’s most vulnerable. Alongside numerous meetings with political and Church representatives, Prevost will attend a gathering in Lima on “the challenges and hopes for the future of the Peruvian people”, together with his friend Cardinal Carlos Castillo.He will meet young people and university students at the capital’s stadium, fly to the open-air site of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, travel up into the highlands to the Indigenous city of Cuzco and reach Pucallpa, on the edge of the Amazon rainforest. Initially, he had to contend with a hostile environment heavily dominated by Opus Dei.He recalled Chiclayo from the balcony of St Peter’s Basilica on the very evening of his election, after the white smoke had announced the choice of a new Pope. There, he will be reunited with many friends and members of the faithful, dine with priests, celebrate Mass and once again walk the streets, squares and buildings so familiar to him.In Peru, and possibly at other stops on the journey, the Pope is also expected to meet victims of abuse within the Peruvian Church. As a cardinal, working alongside Francis, Prevost helped dissolve the conservative Sodalitium Christianae Vitae movement. On Monday 16 November, he will board his return flight, arriving in Rome on the morning of Tuesday 17 November.
summary: Over 12 days, Robert Francis Prevost will travel more than 30,000 kilometres, visit 14 locations, take numerous flights by plane and helicopter, attend more than 50 engagements and deliver around 40 speeches.It is a demanding, tightly packed schedule that Leo XIV was determined not to alter after undergoing successful surgery on 13 October to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung.
